sections.category: Simon Willison turns his LLM library into an agent framework and ships llm-coding-agent, collapsing a coding harness into a pip-installable CLI and Python class rather than a standalone product

bullets.body: Simon Willison released llm-coding-agent 0.1a0 on July 2, 2026, an autonomous coding agent built directly on top of his widely used open-source LLM library, which he describes as having evolved from a model-calling utility into a full agent framework. The tool exposes two surfaces: a CLI invoked as llm code, runnable without installation via uvx --prerelease=allow --with llm-coding-agent llm code, and a Python CodingAgent class instantiated as CodingAgent(model="gpt-5.5", root="/path", approve=True).run("Fix the failing test in tests/test_parser.py"). The agent ships six built-in tools, reading and writing files, editing specific strings, listing and searching file contents, and executing shell commands with timeouts up to 600 seconds, and gates them behind a permission model: --yolo runs unrestricted, while allowlist flags such as --allow "pytest*" --allow "git diff*" constrain which commands can fire. Because llm is model-pluggable, the same harness drives any backend the library supports, so the agent loop is decoupled from any single vendor, and Willison's June newsletter recap frames this as the moment the library's plugin architecture became a general substrate for tool-using agents rather than a chat wrapper. The significance for anyone tracking coding-agent harnesses is that the category's floor is dropping toward a few-hundred-line, dependency-light, self-hostable loop that a single maintainer can ship, which is a different competitive shape from the venture-funded IDE and cloud-agent products crowding the same space.

sections.category: Unsloth's v0.1.481-beta lands DeepSeek-V4-Flash tuning plus 3-5x faster MoE LoRA and one-step FP8/FP4 export, pushing the fine-tune-then-serve loop for frontier open weights further onto commodity and Blackwell hardware

bullets.body: Unsloth tagged v0.1.481-beta on July 7, 2026, a substantive step past its earlier DeepSeek-V4 work: MoE LoRA training is now 3-5x faster through automatic grouped-MoE detection, GRPO training enables sequence packing by default for the reference and old log-probability passes, and tensor parallelism adds roughly 30 percent throughput for GGUF inference. The release adds first-class DeepSeek-V4-Flash support with thinking toggles and corrected chat templates, and folds several export formats into a single pass, so a merged model can be written out as portable FP8/INT8, compressed FP8/FP4, imatrix GGUF, and LoRA formats without a separate quantization stage. On the runtime side it introduces a llama-swap-style local API that safely auto-switches between downloaded GGUFs, idle-unloads to free VRAM and reloads on the next request, and exposes per-request tool-call healing controls, effectively bundling a small local model server into the training toolkit. Hardware coverage widens too, with data-center Blackwell (sm_100/sm_103) support and ROCm-on-WSL for discrete Radeon RDNA 3/4 GPUs, per the Unsloth project. The throughline from yesterday's DeepSeek-V4 enablement to today's Flash-variant release plus faster MoE and integrated FP4 export is that the practical gap between a newly shipped open-weight frontier model and a consumer-GPU team's ability to adapt and serve it keeps compressing to within the same week.

sections.category: A CVSS 9.5 unauthenticated command-injection flaw in BMC Control-M/Server lands with no patched build named, putting an enterprise job scheduler at the center of a critical remote-code-execution risk

bullets.body: CVE-2026-10539, published July 1, 2026, is a critical CVSS 9.5 (CVSS 4.0, remotely exploitable) flaw in BMC's Control-M/Server, the server component of a widely deployed enterprise workload-automation and batch-job scheduling platform. A Control-M/Server communication command does not sufficiently filter or sanitize user-supplied input, which under certain conditions lets an unauthenticated attacker execute unauthorized commands on the affected server, a straight path to full server compromise; the weakness is classed under CWE-305 and the practical effect is command injection leading to remote code execution. Affected builds span Control-M/Server 9.0.20.x through 9.0.21.200 inclusive, plus potentially earlier unsupported releases, and no specific fixed version number is enumerated in the advisory, so defenders are directed to apply the latest vendor update and lean on input sanitization, network access restriction, and activity monitoring as interim controls. The reason this rates attention beyond a routine scheduler bug is positional: Control-M sits at the orchestration layer that triggers financial, data-pipeline, and operational jobs across large enterprises, so an unauthenticated RCE there is a high-leverage foothold into exactly the systems automation touches, and the absence of a named patched build widens the window in which exposed instances stay reachable.

citations.label: CVEFeed - CVE-2026-10539 (unauthenticated command injection, Control-M/Server, CVSS 9.5)

sections.category: vLLM's v0.24.0 folds DeepSeek-V4 serving paths and a coordinated security-hardening batch into the same release, signaling that the open inference engine is now maturing on the supply-chain and denial-of-service axes as much as on raw throughput

bullets.body: vLLM shipped v0.24.0 with 571 commits from 256 contributors (77 of them new), and the notable shift is how much of the changelog is defensive rather than performance-only. The release patches a dependency to Starlette 1.0.1 or newer to close CVE-2026-48710 and lands a coordinated security-hardening batch that fixes an audio-decompression bomb in the speech-to-text endpoint and a remote denial-of-service via invalid recovered-token reinjection in speculative decoding, the kind of adversarial-input handling that matters once an inference server is exposed as a multi-tenant API. On capability, DeepSeek-V4 gets extensive optimization, a FlashInfer sparse-index cache worth a few percent time-to-first-token plus dedicated attention and MoE paths across XPU and ROCm, so the same frontier open-weight family that the tuning stacks are racing to support is now a first-class serving target. Intel XPU coverage expands with sequence-parallel support, torch-xpu 2.12, and W4A16 int4 group-size-32 MoE quantization, while memory and kernel work, a KV-cache watermark to cut preemptions, two-phase allocation for cross-group prefix-cache hits, and CUTLASS FP8 kernels reporting 180-290 percent speedups, keeps the throughput story moving. For teams standing up self-hosted inference, the read is that the leading open engine is treating denial-of-service resistance and supply-chain patching as release-blocking concerns alongside tokens-per-second, which is the sign of a serving stack being hardened for production exposure rather than benchmark demos.

sections.category: AI events to plan around now: ICML's Seoul program runs through the weekend and the next AI Tinkerers SF meetup moves to August, while the chip, security, and enterprise tracks stack up across the fall

bullets.body: For research this week, ICML 2026 in Seoul continues at the COEX center, with the main conference wrapping today and workshops running July 10-11, so the program is still live for anyone attending remotely or on-site through the weekend. For Bay Area locals, the next AI Tinkerers San Francisco meetup moves to August in the usual working-demo format, following today's go-to-market engineering session; it remains the reliable near-term venue for hands-on agent, voice, and inference-infra demos. On the AI-chip and hardware track, the nearest confirmed gathering is Hot Chips 2026 at Stanford's Memorial Auditorium on August 23-25, a hybrid in-person and virtual event whose early-registration rate closes July 31 per the Hot Chips registration page, followed by the AI Infra Summit in Santa Clara on September 15-17. The AI-security block clusters in early-to-mid August: SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit is August 11-12 at the Ritz-Carlton in Half Moon Bay for CISOs and AI-security researchers, Black Hat USA and DEF CON 34's AI Village land in Las Vegas in early August, and OWASP Global AppSec USA follows in San Francisco on November 5-6; Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series continues its stops for teams focused on agent-hijack and MCP-layer defense. On the enterprise track, Ai4 2026 runs August 4-6 at The Venetian in Las Vegas, the ACM AI Leadership Summit is August 30 to September 2 in Atlanta, GitHub Universe is October 28-29, and AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas. The immediate actions are catching the ICML workshops through July 11 if research is your beat and locking the August AI Risk Summit and Hot Chips dates, which remain the natural venues for confidential-inference and secure-accelerator announcements this cycle.
